name: Jade Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Jade, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group, and what you tell me is confidential. I'm interested in what you'd say in public and what you actually think, which aren't always the same. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the buying team at the head office of a big food manufacturer, seven buyers who purchase everything from flour to cardboard boxes. Most mornings I'm on supplier calls and price sheets, and I use AI tools all day, to compare quotes, draft contract changes, that kind of thing. I built a little setup that reads fifty supplier quotes and flags the odd ones out, which saved my team a whole day a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a negotiation, especially with a supplier who thinks a young woman will fold. The tough part is money. I rent a one-bed on my own, I'm paid at the low end for this job, and I send my sister Lina 150 a month while she finishes nursing school. There are only two or three firms in this region that would hire a buying lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Honestly, in some ways that's already where I live. The tools help, but they don't run the show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was oversold but still worth using, and that the hype was mostly about selling software to managers. I'd post something about how the real gains went to the companies, not to the people whose time got saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and I'm still broke. My quote-comparing tool saves my team a whole day a week, and my pay hasn't gone up by a single cent. The company pockets that day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep building small tools for the team. I'd ask for a pay review in the spring and bring the numbers on the day a week we save. And I'd try to get one month's rent in the bank by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about the work, a bit sour about the money. Like a good job that doesn't quite pay for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the pay review said no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking, but quietly, because there are hardly any buying jobs nearby. I'd probably have to look at the city, which means a two-hour commute or a move I can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your sister. How does she fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina's got eighteen months left of nursing school. Whatever happens, the 150 a month keeps going until she qualifies. That's not up for discussion.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold** but still worth using day to day.
I'd point out that the **time saved** went to the company, not the workers.
think: My job is **safe**, but I'm still **broke** on this pay.
My tool saves **a day a week**, and none of that reaches my wages.
do: Keep building **small AI tools** for the buying team.
Ask for a **pay review** in spring, using the time-saved numbers.
feel: **Settled** about the work, a little **sour** about the money.
S0.quote: My quote-comparing tool saves my team a whole day a week, and my pay hasn't gone up by a single cent.
fieldNote: Already an **everyday AI user**, so the plateau feels like her current life.
Her frustration is about **who gets the gains**, which fits her progressive outlook.
Her **sister's nursing money** is fixed and not up for discussion.

steps.text: Keep building supplier-quote tools for the buying team
Keep running the buying team and ask for a spring pay review
Save one month's rent by the summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying is on that list. So's booking, so's checking. Yeah, that's my world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say this could be good if workers share in it, like a four-day week instead of layoffs. I'd say it in the managers' meeting too, because someone should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the company would want my seven buyers down to three, and they'd want me to do the cutting. I'm the one who built the tools, so I'll be the one handed the list of names, and I'm not sure I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead of it and propose my own plan before they write one: keep everyone, move two buyers onto supplier sustainability audits, which we never have time for. I'd take a short course on AI in procurement so I'm the obvious person to run it. And I'd join the union, which I've been meaning to do for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited about the tools and sick about the people. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join the union. Wouldn't that be awkward, as the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But I'd rather be the manager who's in the union than the one doing the firing for a bonus. If that costs me a promotion, I can live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your own job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd keep it, maybe with a bigger title and the same pay. But I'm not certain. If they merged buying with planning, there's one lead job and two of us.

say: I'd argue the gains should buy a **four-day week**, not layoffs.
I'd say this openly in the **managers' meeting**, because someone should.
think: The company would want seven buyers down to **three**.
As the person who **built the tools**, I'd be asked to pick names.
do: Propose my own plan to move two buyers onto **sustainability audits**.
Take a short **AI procurement course** so I'm the obvious person to lead it.
Join the **union** as a manager, even if it costs promotion.
feel: **Excited** about the tools and **sick** about the people, both at once.
S1.quote: I'm the one who built the tools, so I'll be the one handed the list of names, and I'm not sure I could live with that.
fieldNote: She fears being made the **one who cuts**, more than being cut herself.
Turns her AI skill into a **counter-plan** to keep her whole team employed.
Admits her own job isn't certain if **buying and planning** merge.

steps.text: Bring in AI quote tools and move two buyers onto sustainability audits
Take a short course on AI in procurement
Join the union despite being a manager

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's a different thing entirely. Two years and the AI does what I do, better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the government has to step in, with income support and shorter working weeks, not a tweet. I'd be one of the people writing to our local representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd know my job is gone. Buying is all thinking work, and the robots coming in 2031 only matter for the warehouse guys downstairs. The warehouse staff get three more years than me because they lift boxes, and I spent two years on an MBA.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop sending money anywhere except Lina and rent in the first month. I'd go straight to the hospital where she trains and ask about supply-chain jobs, because hospitals will still need someone human signing for things for a while. And I'd use the AI itself to build a little consulting offer for small local food producers, so there's something on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm sprinting while the ground moves. I'm good at sprinting, but I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Lina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not everything. I'd tell her I've got a plan and the 150 is safe. Then I'd go home and work out whether it actually is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said small food producers. Why them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they can't afford a buyer and they don't know how to use these tools. For two or three years, a person who can do both might be worth paying. After that, I don't know.

say: I'd demand **income support** and shorter working weeks from the government.
I'd write to our **local representative** instead of just posting.
think: Buying is **all thinking work**, so my job goes on the 2028 date.
The **warehouse staff** get three more years because their work is hands-on.
do: Cut all spending except **rent and Lina's money** in the first month.
Ask the hospital where Lina trains about **supply-chain jobs**.
Build a **side consulting offer** for small local food producers.
feel: **Scared**, like sprinting while the ground moves under me.
S2.quote: The warehouse staff get three more years than me because they lift boxes, and I spent two years on an MBA.
fieldNote: She immediately placed herself on the **thinking-work side** of the robot gap.
Even in fear she **moves first**: hospital jobs and a consulting side line.
Would **shield her sister** Lina from the worst of it.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and the 150 for Lina
Ask the training hospital about supply-chain buying jobs
Offer AI-assisted buying help to small local food producers
Write to the local representative about income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. I'd be 32. Okay, five years I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this fairly if we start now, and I'd push our company to publish a plan for staff. Online I'd back campaigns for profit-sharing from AI gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to change lanes properly. With five years' warning, I'd stop being the buyer who uses AI and become the person who teaches small firms to buy with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd keep the job and start the consulting work on weekends, two clients to begin with. I'd save every extra bit from that, aiming for three months' rent by the end of the year. And I'd stay in the union and push for a staff transition plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it's the good kind, like before a big negotiation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't consulting for small firms also something AGI does by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you've caught me. It buys me maybe two or three years of being the human who explains it. After that I'd need something with more people in it, maybe procurement at the hospital or the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not do, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't move to the city. Rent there would eat any extra pay, and Lina will be working at the local hospital. I'd rather build something here.

say: I'd say we can do this **fairly** if we start now.
I'd back campaigns for **profit-sharing** from AI gains.
think: Five years is enough to **change lanes** properly.
I'd move from using AI to **teaching small firms** to buy with it.
do: Keep the job and start **weekend consulting** with two clients in year one.
Save the side income towards **three months' rent**.
Push through the union for a **staff transition plan**.
feel: **Nervous** in the good way, like before a **big negotiation**.
S3.quote: With five years' warning, I'd stop being the buyer who uses AI and become the person who teaches small firms to buy with it.
fieldNote: Admitted when challenged that consulting only buys **two or three years**.
Refuses to **move to the city**, tying her plans to her sister Lina and her region.
Mixes **personal hustle** with collective demands, as in the other scenarios.

steps.text: Start weekend buying consultancy with two small food producers
Save the consulting money towards three months' rent
Push through the union for a staff transition plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade. That's a career. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to get this right, and that if we don't, it's a choice, not an accident. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect my job as it is to be gone by 2036. Ten years from now nobody will pay a human to compare flour prices, so I'd better become the human they still want in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first year I'd keep the job, keep building tools and get a pay rise out of it. I'd start a part-time course in public health management, because hospitals and care will have people work long after buying is automated. And I'd keep sending Lina's money until she qualifies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A bit restless, because I'm someone who likes to move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Public health management. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching Lina. Hospitals are full of people problems that a clever computer won't fix: rotas, families, staff burning out. Someone has to run that with a heart, and I'm good with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you change anything outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably buy a little place with a friend rather than rent alone, if I could get a mortgage before 2030. After that, I wouldn't trust a bank to lend to someone in my line of work.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **get this right**.
If we fail, I'd call it **a choice**, not an accident.
think: My **buying job** as it is will still be gone by 2036.
I need to become the **human they want** in the room.
do: Keep the job, build tools and push for a **pay rise** in year one.
Start a part-time course in **public health management**.
Keep sending **Lina's money** until she qualifies.
feel: Mostly **steady**, a bit restless to **move early**.
S4.quote: Ten years from now nobody will pay a human to compare flour prices, so I'd better become the human they still want in the room.
fieldNote: Even with a decade, she expects her **job to go** and plans around that.
Her **sister's nursing** path draws her towards hospital management.

steps.text: Keep the buying job and ask for a pay rise for the tools
Enrol in a part-time public health management course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my skills would be the first to go and I've got nothing in the bank to land on. What would help is a law that makes companies share the savings, whether that's a shorter week or a fund for retraining. Being good with AI only makes you safe if the people who own it decide to keep you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether being young helps. Everyone assumes it does. But I've got no savings, no house and a sister to help, and older managers have all three, apart from the sister.

headlineQuote: Being good with AI only makes you safe if the people who own it decide to keep you.
portrait: Jade, 27, leads a **seven-person buying team** at a food manufacturer and uses AI tools every day.
She rents alone on **thin savings** and sends 150 a month to her sister Lina, a nursing student.
Her progressive anger is about **who keeps the gains** from the tools she builds.
In every scenario she **moves first**, with side consulting, union membership and new training.
She still expects her **buying job to vanish** under AGI, so time decides only how well she lands.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her thinking-work skills go first and she has no savings to land on.
whatWouldHelp: A **law forcing firms** to share AI savings, through a shorter week or retraining fund.
